title: Cryptographic Hash Function
body:
A function $H$ taking a message of any length to a fixed-length digest, designed so that **you
cannot work backwards and cannot find two inputs that agree**.

$$H : \{0,1\}^* \to \{0,1\}^n, \qquad n = 256 \text{ or } 512$$

It is the workhorse of applied cryptography: password storage, [[Digital Signature|signatures]],
[[HMAC|message authentication]], commitment, blockchains, `git` object IDs, and file integrity all
sit on one. Unlike everything in [[Public Key Cryptography]] it has no key and no secret.

## Not the same thing as a hash table's hash function

**The trap of the course, and the vault contains both notes.** [[Hashing]] in
[[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] (COMP 2631) opens with "searching is the problem; hashing is the refusal
to search" and optimises for speed and even spread. That function and this one share a name and
almost nothing else:

| | [[Hashing]] (COMP 2631) | Cryptographic hash (here) |
|---|---|---|
| Wants | speed, uniform spread over $m$ buckets | pre-image and collision resistance |
| Collisions | **expected**, handled by chaining | a **break** of the function |
| Output size | table-sized, $h(k) = k \bmod m$ | fixed and large, 256+ bits |
| Invertible | irrelevant, often trivially so | must not be, at any cost |
| Speed | as fast as possible | deliberately slow for passwords |
| Adversary | none, keys are just data | assumed, funded, and clever |

`k mod m` is a perfectly good hash function for a [[Hashing|hash table]] and a catastrophic one here: it is
inverted by inspection. Conversely SHA-256 would be an absurd choice for a hash table, thousands of
times slower than needed to solve a problem that has no adversary. **Same word, opposite design
brief.**

## The three resistances

They climb, and the names get confused constantly, so keep the quantifiers straight.

| Property | Given | Find | Generic cost |
|---|---|---|--:|
| **Pre-image resistance** | a digest $y$ | any $m$ with $H(m) = y$ | $2^n$ |
| **Second pre-image resistance** | a message $m_1$ | $m_2 \ne m_1$ with $H(m_2) = H(m_1)$ | $2^n$ |
| **Collision resistance** | nothing | any $m_1 \ne m_2$ with $H(m_1) = H(m_2)$ | $2^{n/2}$ |

The difference between the last two is who chooses the messages. Second pre-image is handed a
target; collision resistance lets the attacker pick *both* sides, which is far easier, and it is
the strongest of the three: collision resistance implies second pre-image resistance.

**Collisions cost only $2^{n/2}$ because of the birthday paradox**, the same argument
[[Hashing]] uses to explain why collision resolution is mandatory rather than a fallback: what grows
is the number of **pairs**, $\binom{n}{2}$, not the number of items. See [[Combination]] and
[[Probability]]. This is why digests are twice as long as the security level you want: SHA-256
gives 128 bits of collision resistance, not 256.

Collisions **must** exist, by pigeonhole: the domain is infinite and the range is not. The claim is
only that finding one is infeasible.

## Construction

**Merkle-Damgård** is the classical design and covers MD5, SHA-1, and SHA-2. Chop the padded
message into blocks and iterate a fixed *compression function* $f$:

```
IV --f--> h1 --f--> h2 --f--> ... --> hk = digest
     ^         ^         ^
    m1        m2        mk
```

The theorem that makes it worth doing: **if $f$ is collision resistant, so is the whole
construction.** Building a good fixed-size compression function is a tractable engineering problem;
this reduces the variable-length problem to it. The padding must encode the message length
(Merkle-Damgård strengthening) or the reduction fails.

Its known flaw is the **length-extension attack**: the digest *is* the internal state, so given
$H(m)$ and $|m|$, an attacker can compute $H(m \| \text{pad} \| m')$ without knowing $m$. That
breaks the naive MAC $H(k \| m)$ and is the reason [[HMAC]] exists.

**SHA-3** (Keccak, 2015) is not Merkle-Damgård at all. It uses a *sponge*: absorb the message into
a large internal state by XOR-and-permute, then squeeze output out of it. The state is bigger than
the output, so length extension is structurally impossible. SHA-3 was standardised as insurance
after SHA-1 fell, not because SHA-2 was broken; SHA-2 is fine and is still the default.

| Function | Digest | Status |
|---|--:|---|
| MD5 | 128 | **broken**, collisions in seconds |
| SHA-1 | 160 | **broken**, SHAttered 2017 |
| SHA-2 (SHA-256/512) | 256/512 | fine, the current default |
| SHA-3 (Keccak) | 224-512 | fine, different construction |

## What it is used for

- **Signatures.** You sign $H(m)$, not $m$: it is faster, it fits the modulus, and it is why a
  collision is a forgery. See [[Digital Signature]].
- **Message authentication.** [[HMAC]], with a key.
- **Password storage.** Never store the password; store $H(\text{salt} \| \text{password})$. Here
  you want the hash **slow**, which is the exact opposite of the hash table requirement, so use
  bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2 rather than SHA-256. The salt defeats precomputed rainbow tables.
- **Commitment and integrity.** Publish $H(m)$ now, reveal $m$ later, and you cannot change your
  mind. A `git` commit ID and a Merkle tree are this idea repeated.
- **Key derivation.** Turning the structured group element out of [[Diffie-Hellman]] into a uniform
  [[AES]] key.

A hash gives **integrity, not confidentiality and not authenticity**. Anyone can recompute
$H(m)$, so an attacker who changes the message changes the digest to match. Detecting tampering
needs a secret, which is the whole reason for [[HMAC]].
